## Predicting the Demand for Rented Bikes in Seoul Considering Time and Weather Variables

---

# Purpose of Predictive Question

- Help maintain a stable supply of bikes for bike-renters.

- May be used to project revenues for companies offering bikes for renting.

---

# Raw Data

- Seoul bikes data set has 8760 observations and 14 features (variables).

- Variables are: Rented Bike Count, Hour, Holiday, Temperature(°C), Humidity (%), Rainfall(mm), Snowfall(cm) and other weather-related variables.

```{r}
seoul_bikes_raw |> 
  head(n = 10)
```

---

# Bike Demand vs. Temperature
```{r warning=FALSE, echo=FALSE, message=FALSE, fig.width = 9}
seoul_bikes <- seoul_bikes |> 
  mutate(
    peak = ifelse(hour %in% c(7:9, 17:19), TRUE, FALSE)
    #used Gemini to help with shortening the conditional statement, as initially was hour == 7 | hour == 8 | ... 
  )

seoul_bikes |> 
  ggplot(aes(x = temperature_c, y = rented_bike_count)) +
  geom_jitter(
    aes(colour = peak),
    alpha = 0.15
  ) +
  geom_smooth(
    method = "gam",
    se = FALSE,
    linewidth = 1.2,
    colour = "#d95f02"
    ) +
  facet_grid( #changed to facet_grid to take holidays into account, not taking weekdays vs. weekends into account as there many weekend workers in Seoul who may need to commute
    holiday ~ peak,
    labeller = as_labeller(c("TRUE" = "Peak", "FALSE" = "Non-Peak", "Holiday" = "Holiday", "No Holiday" = "Working Day"))
    ) +
  #changes labels from facetting to "Peak" and "Non-Peak"
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(
    panel.spacing.x = unit(1.5, "cm") # Increases horizontal gap between the two columns
  ) +
  scale_colour_manual(
    guide = "legend",
    values = c("TRUE" = "#384860", "FALSE" = "#97a6c4"), #changed colour to lighter shades, as otherwise points are too dark
    labels = c("TRUE" = "Peak", "FALSE" = "Non-Peak")
    ) +
  guides(alpha = "none") +
  labs(
    x = "Temperature (c)",
    y = "Number of Rented Bikes Per Hour",
    colour = "Peak Commuting Hour (7-9am or 5-7pm)",
    title = "Bike Demand vs. Temperature"
  )
```

---

# Bike Demand vs. Seasons

```{r warning=FALSE, echo=FALSE, message=FALSE}
hourly_holiday_comparison <- seoul_bikes %>%
  group_by(seasons, holiday, hour) %>%
  summarise(
    avg_rentals = mean(rented_bike_count, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
   )

ggplot(hourly_holiday_comparison,
       aes(x = hour, y = avg_rentals,
           colour = holiday)) +
  # Used geom_line() instead of geom_col() because I'm now investigating how rentals change throughout the day.
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) +
  # Used facet_wrap() for easier comparison
  facet_wrap(
    ~factor(seasons,
                      levels = c("Winter", "Spring",
                                 "Summer", "Autumn")),
    #added axes = "all_x" by asking GenAi because I wanted all graphs to have x-axis only the bottom 2 originally had it.
    axes = "all_x"
  )+
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(0, 23, 3)) +

  labs(
    title = "Hourly average bike rentals by season and type of holiday",
    x = "Hour of day",
    y = "Average number of bikes rented",
    colour = "Holiday type"
  ) +
  theme_minimal() 
```

---


# Bike Demand vs. Precipitation (Rainfall)

```{r warning=FALSE, echo=FALSE, message=FALSE}
# Rainfall box plot: exclude snow to isolate rainfall
# 3.4 Compare rain and snow separately, keeping dry hours in both plots.
rain_data <- seoul_bikes %>%
  filter(snowfall_cm == 0)

# Define precipitation bands
rain_data <- rain_data %>%
  mutate(
    rain_level = case_when(
      rainfall_mm == 0 ~ "0",
      rainfall_mm > 0 & rainfall_mm <= 1 ~ "(0, 1]",
      rainfall_mm > 1 & rainfall_mm <= 5 ~ "(1, 5]",
      rainfall_mm > 5 & rainfall_mm <= 10 ~ "(5, 10]",
      rainfall_mm > 10 ~ ">10"
    ),
    rain_level = fct_relevel(
      rain_level,
      "0", "(0, 1]", "(1, 5]", "(5, 10]", ">10"
    )
  )


# Rainfall box plot: exclude snow to isolate rainfall
ggplot(
  data = rain_data,
  mapping = aes(x = rain_level, y = rented_bike_count)
) +
  geom_boxplot(fill = "lightblue") +
  theme_minimal() +
  labs(
    title = "Bike rentals by rainfall level",
    x = "Rainfall (mm)",
    y = "Hourly bike rentals"
  )
```

---


# Bike Demand vs. Precipitation (Snowfall)

```{r warning=FALSE, echo=FALSE, message=FALSE}
snow_data <- seoul_bikes %>%
  filter(rainfall_mm == 0)

snow_data <- snow_data %>%
  mutate(
    snow_level = case_when(
      snowfall_cm == 0 ~ "0",
      snowfall_cm > 0 & snowfall_cm <= 1 ~ "(0, 1]",
      snowfall_cm > 1 & snowfall_cm <= 3 ~ "(1, 3]",
      snowfall_cm > 3 & snowfall_cm <= 5 ~ "(3, 5]",
      snowfall_cm > 5 ~ ">5"
    ),
    snow_level = fct_relevel(
      snow_level,
      "0", "(0, 1]", "(1, 3]", "(3, 5]", ">5"
    )
  )

# Snowfall box plot: exclude rain to isolate snowfall
ggplot(
  data = snow_data,
  mapping = aes(x = snow_level, y = rented_bike_count)
) +
  theme_minimal() +
  geom_boxplot(fill = "lightgrey") +
  labs(
    title = "Bike rentals by snowfall level",
    x = "Snowfall (cm)",
    y = "Hourly bike rentals"
  )
  
```

---

# Feature Engineering & Model Preperation

- Created precipitation variable - combined rainfall_mm and snowfall_cm for simplicity.

- Introduced is_weekend variable - determines if the day is in the week or in the weekend.

- Factorised hour variable

- Variables for model: rented_bike_count, hour, holiday, is_weekend, temperature_c, humidity_percent, seasons, precipitation.
---

# Linear Model

$$
\begin{aligned}
\widehat{\text{rented_bike_count}} &= 728.63 -68.83 \times \text{is_weekend} + 20.48 \times \text{temperature_c} - 6.73 \times \text{humidity_percent} \\
&\quad - 245.86 \times \text{precipitation} - 99.47 \times \text{hour_X1} - 197.92 \times \text{hour_X2} + \dots \\
&\quad + 153.47 \times \text{holiday_No.Holiday} - 66.23 \times \text{seasons_Spring} + 10.31 \times \text{seasons_Summer} \\
&\quad - 282.22 \times \text{seasons_Winter}
\end{aligned}
$$
- 32 terms
- seaons_Autumn and other terms that seem missing are 'absorbed' into baseline

---

# Model Evaluation

```{r, echo = FALSE}
seoul_bikes_clean <- seoul_bikes |> 
  mutate(
    precipitation = ifelse(rainfall_mm > 0 | snowfall_cm > 0, 1, 0),
    is_weekend   = wday(dmy(date)) %in% c(1, 7),
    #hour_holiday = interaction(hour, holiday, sep = "_")
    hour = as.factor(hour)
  ) |> 
  select(
    rented_bike_count,
    #hour_holiday,
    hour,
    holiday,
    is_weekend,
    temperature_c,
    humidity_percent,
    seasons,
    precipitation
  )

set.seed(67)

seoul_bikes_clean_split <- initial_split(seoul_bikes_clean, prop = 0.80)

train_data <- training(seoul_bikes_clean_split)
test_data <- testing(seoul_bikes_clean_split)

seoul_bikes_rec_2 <- recipe(
  rented_bike_count ~ .,
  data = train_data
) |> 
  step_dummy(all_nominal(), -all_outcomes()) |>
  step_zv(all_predictors())

seoul_bikes_mod <- linear_reg() |> 
  set_engine("lm")

seoul_bikes_wflow_2 <- workflow() |> 
  add_model(seoul_bikes_mod) |> 
  add_recipe(seoul_bikes_rec_2)

seoul_bikes_fit_2 <- seoul_bikes_wflow_2 |> 
  fit(data = train_data)

seoul_bikes_pred_2 <- predict(seoul_bikes_fit_2, new_data = test_data) |> 
  bind_cols(test_data |> select(rented_bike_count))

bikes_metrics <- metric_set(rmse, rsq)

eval_model <- function(pred_df, wflow, model){
  std_metrics <- pred_df |> 
    bikes_metrics(truth = rented_bike_count, estimate = .pred) |> 
    select(.metric, .estimate) |> 
    pivot_wider(names_from = .metric, values_from = .estimate)
  
  n <- nrow(pred_df)
  p <- nrow(tidy(wflow)) - 1 #-1 because of the baseline
  min <- min(pred_df$rented_bike_count)
  max <- max(pred_df$rented_bike_count)
  
  std_metrics |> 
    mutate(
      model = model,
      num_terms = p+1, #+1 here as the total number of terms includes the baseline
      adj_rsq = 1 - ((1 - rsq) * (n-1)) / (n - p - 1),
      min = min,
      max = max
    ) |> 
    select(model, num_terms, rmse, min, max, rsq, adj_rsq)
}

eval_model(seoul_bikes_pred_2, seoul_bikes_fit_2, "Model 2") |> 
  kable(digits = 4, caption = "Model Evaluation Metrics (Testing Data)")
```

# Residual Graph
```{r warning=FALSE, echo=FALSE, message=FALSE}
seoul_bikes_aug <- augment(
     seoul_bikes_fit_2,
     new_data = train_data)

ggplot(seoul_bikes_aug, aes(x = .pred, y = .resid)) +
     geom_point(alpha = 0.5) +
     geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", color = "gray") +
     labs(
         x = "Predicted Rental Bike Count",
         y = "Residuals",
         title = "Residuals vs Predicted Rental Bike Count"
     ) +
  theme_minimal()

seoul_bikes_aug_test <- augment(
  seoul_bikes_fit_2,
  new_data = test_data)

ggplot(seoul_bikes_aug_test, aes(x = .pred, y = .resid)) +
     geom_point(alpha = 0.5) +
     geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", color = "gray") +
     labs(
       x = "Predicted Rental Bike Count (Test Data)", 
       y = "Residuals",
       title = "Residuals vs Predicted Bike Count (Test Data)"
     ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

---

# Limitations

1. **Non-linear relationships**: bike demand responds non-linearly to predictors e.g. temperature, hour of day, precipitation.

2. **Loss of precipitation accuracy**: collapsing rainfall and snowfall into a binary variable sacrifices the granularity regarding weather severities.

3. **Impossible negative predictions**: model can predict negative bike counts, which are impossible, considering real values are above 0

4. **Omitted contextual variables**: e.g. public transport disruptions, major local events etc. leaves approximately 42.5% of variance unexplained.

---
# Conclusion
Overall, our investigation demonstrated that both time and weather variables are useful in predicting bike rental demand in Seoul. Demand is generally higher during warmer weather, summer months and peak commuting hours, while rainfall, snowfall and colder temperatures are associated with lower demand. Our linear regression model achieved a testing R-squared value of 0.575, indicating moderate predictive performance. Hypothesis testing also showed that 26 out of 31 slope coefficients were statistically significant at the 5% significance level before adjusting for multiple testing. However, the model has several limitations, including non-linear relationships, loss of information regarding precipitation severity and negative predictions. Despite these limitations, our model provides a useful starting point for predicting bike rental demand, which could help bike rental companies manage their bike supply and estimate future revenues. Further improvements could be made by incorporating additional variables and exploring more flexible modelling techniques.
